title: Creation of Hangul (Hunminjeongeum)
summary: In 1443 King Sejong and his scholars created the Korean alphabet, later called Hangul, and in 1446 it was promulgated in the book Hunminjeongeum, "the proper sounds for instructing the people". It originally had 28 letters, of which 24 are used today. The book was registered in UNESCO's Memory of the World in October 1997.

uncertainty.note: Created 1443 and promulgated 1446 in the sources; one source (Korean Cultural Center New York) says Sejong promulgated it in 1443.

where.modern_name: Gyeongbokgung, Seoul (proxy pin for the royal court; the sources do not name the work site)
where.historical_name: Hanyang, Joseon Korea (royal court of King Sejong)

importance.justification: Origin of the native Korean writing system, used by the Korean language today.

reviewer_note: Creation 1443 vs promulgation 1446 is a source disagreement (KCC NY says 1443 promulgation). Pin is a proxy at the royal palace; no source opened says where in the capital the work was done. Letter counts (28 original, 24 used) are from the Korea Herald; Korea.net counts 14 consonants plus 10 vowels.
